topic: SC: a public servant arrested and kept in judicial custody for more than 48 hours is under deemed suspension - no separate order needed; bail ordinarily granted in such Prevention of Corruption Act cases unless criminal antecedents or very gross facts; bribe amount not a relevant factor for bail; Patna HC order cancelling bail set aside (Vishwajeet Singh @ Bishwajeet Ramanand v. State of Bihar, Crl. A. 5282/2026, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1146, Justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan, 6 Nov 2026)

slides.title: In custody over **48 hours**? Deemed suspended
slides.subtitle: A public servant arrested and kept in judicial custody for **more than 48 hours** is treated as suspended, even without a written order, says the Supreme Court.
slides.cite: **Vishwajeet Singh @ Bishwajeet Ramanand v. State of Bihar** · Crl. A. 5282/2026 · 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1146 · Justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan · 6 Nov 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: A Rs 4,000 **bribe case**
bullets: A hospital manager in Samastipur, Bihar, was accused of demanding **Rs 4,000** to clear a worker's wages of Rs 36,421.
He was booked under the **Prevention of Corruption Act**, spent about **15 days** in judicial custody, and got bail from the Sessions Court.
Almost **a year later**, the Patna High Court cancelled his bail on the complainant's plea.

slides.label: Deemed suspension
slides.title: No **separate order** needed
bullets: Once a public servant is arrested and stays in judicial custody for **over 48 hours**, the suspension happens **automatically**.
The department does **not** have to pass a specific order for it.
Here, the State had revoked his suspension and posted him back to the **same hospital and post**. The Court called this disturbing and asked the State to review it.
slides.note: **Note:** the Court did not itself order a fresh suspension. It asked the State to take steps in accordance with law.

slides.label: On bail
slides.title: Bail **restored**
bullets: In cases of this type, bail should **ordinarily** be granted, keeping in mind the maximum punishment possible.
Bail may be refused where the accused has **criminal antecedents** or the facts are **very gross**.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and **restored** the Sessions Court's bail.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Bail is **not** acquittal
bullets: The order does **not** decide whether the accused took the bribe. The trial will decide that.
The Court agreed that the **size of the bribe**, big or small, is **not a relevant factor** for deciding bail.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Government employee arrested and kept in jail for more than 48 hours? Here is what the Supreme Court says ⚖️🏛️

The Supreme Court has said that once a public servant is arrested and remains in judicial custody for more than 48 hours, he is under "deemed suspension". No separate order is needed for it. The case involved a hospital manager in Samastipur, Bihar, accused under the Prevention of Corruption Act of demanding Rs 4,000 to clear a worker's wages. He spent about 15 days in judicial custody before the Sessions Court gave him bail.

Almost a year later, the Patna High Court cancelled his bail. The Supreme Court set that order aside and restored bail. It said that in cases of this type, bail should ordinarily be granted, keeping in mind the maximum punishment possible, unless the accused has criminal antecedents or the facts are very gross. The Court also agreed that the size of the bribe is not a relevant factor for deciding bail.

The Court was disturbed that the State had revoked his suspension and posted him back to the same hospital and post, and asked the State to look into it. Keep in mind: bail is not acquittal. The order does not decide whether the bribe was taken; the trial will.

Case: Vishwajeet Singh @ Bishwajeet Ramanand v. State of Bihar, Criminal Appeal No. 5282/2026, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1146
Bench: Justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan, Supreme Court, 6 Nov 2026
